items.title: Stefon Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2020
items.q: And the same is true of Marc and Casey. So really when I’m composing it’s not so much that I own the idea... When I bring it in to the other guys in the band

ctx.x: Well keeping a group of musicians together for seventeen years is quite an accomplishment. I mean keeping them together for seven days is sometimes impossible. We all do so many things. When you’re working on a tune, perhaps in a rehearsal, and it’s a composition of yours, how comfortable are you with — I’ll use the word “instructing” or “suggesting” to your fellow musicians how to play? Or perhaps what not to play? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

That’s another great question. I would tell you as an improviser I think our success is predicated upon three fundamental values. Those values are love, trust, and respect. When we walk into a room to learn a new piece of music we are leading with that. I never tell Terreon what to play on the drums. Never. There’s no need because I’ve done it maybe twice over the course of the past seventeen years, and both times what I suggested was nowhere near the level of what he came up with on his own. And the same is true…

Yeah. I thought it was a marvelous — what I heard on the preview — a combination of something that was obviously arranged and written out, but then it veered off, came back, and what you’re talking about, the equal contribution of all the players was very evident. I wanted to ask, this could be like minutiae, but I’m fascinated about musical decisions and orchestrations. There’s a point, I believe it was in the first song which was fairly long. And there’s a drum solo. And everybody in the band except the sax…
